questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: Regarding the long heads of biceps and triceps which of the following is true?
questions.explanation: The tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii arises from the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula and passes intracapsularly across the glenohumeral joint before entering the bicipital groove. In contrast, the long head of the triceps brachii arises from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula entirely extracapsularly.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Arm&cubital Fossa core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following does not connect radius and ulna?
questions.explanation: The annular ligament of the radius encircles the head of the radius and attaches to both the anterior and posterior margins of the radial notch of the ulna; it does not connect the radial bone to the ulnar bone directly along shafts or necks, whereas the oblique cord, interosseous membrane, and quadrate ligament directly unite radius and ulna.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Axilla&brachial Plexus core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following pierces the interosseous membrane?
questions.explanation: The anterior interosseous artery descends on the anterior surface of the interosseous membrane and pierces the interosseous membrane at the upper border of pronator quadratus to enter the posterior compartment of the forearm and anastomose with the posterior interosseous artery and dorsal carpal arch.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Nerves of Upper Limb core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following describes the correct order of the distal row of carpals from lateral to medial?
questions.explanation: From lateral to medial, the bones of the distal carpal row are: Trapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, and Hamate (mnemonic: She Looks Too Pretty, Try To Catch Her; second row = Trapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, Hamate).
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Axilla&brachial Plexus core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are medial rotators of the arm EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Infraspinatus (along with teres minor and posterior deltoid) is a lateral rotator of the arm at the glenohumeral joint. Subscapularis, latissimus dorsi, teres major, pectoralis major, and anterior deltoid are all medial rotators.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: The Back core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: What muscles are necessary to raise the arm above the shoulder?
options: First the supraspinatus, next the deltoid, and then the serratus anterior
First the deltoid, next the supraspinatus, and then the serratus anterior
First the serratus anterior, next the deltoid, and then the supraspinatus
First the deltoid, next the serratus anterior, and then supraspinatus
questions.explanation: Abduction of the upper limb is initiated (0° to 15°) by the supraspinatus muscle; abduction from 15° to 90° is performed by the multipennate middle fibers of the deltoid; full abduction and elevation above the horizontal (>90° to 180°) requires scapular upward rotation produced by the serratus anterior (lower 5 digitations) and trapezius.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Shoulder Region core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: Which rotator cuff muscle does NOT rotate the humerus?
questions.explanation: The supraspinatus initiates abduction of the arm (0-15°) and stabilizes the glenohumeral joint; it does not produce rotation. Subscapularis produces medial rotation; infraspinatus and teres minor produce lateral rotation.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Shoulder Region core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: A patient is asked to abduct the arm 90 degrees and then to extend the flexed forearm against resistance. Which muscle is being tested?
questions.explanation: Active extension of the flexed forearm against examiner resistance specifically tests the motor function and strength of the triceps brachii muscle and its radial nerve innervation (C6, C7, C8).
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Arm&cubital Fossa core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: In respect to movement of the arm at the glenohumeral joint, which of the following movements is correctly paired with its prime mover?
options: Abduction . . . pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi
questions.explanation: Posterior fibers of the deltoid and latissimus dorsi are prime movers for arm extension. Pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi adduct; infraspinatus laterally rotates; subscapularis medially rotates.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Pectoral Region core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following joints is paired correctly with its type?
options: Proximal and distal radioulnar joints . . . condyloid type of synovial joint
Radiocarpal joint . . . pivot type of synovial joint
Intercarpal joints . . . plane type of synovial joints
Metacarpophalangeal joints . . . hinge type of synovial joints
Interphalangeal joints . . . condyloid type of synovial joints
questions.explanation: Intercarpal joints are plane synovial joints allowing gliding movements. Radioulnar joints are pivot synovial; radiocarpal is ellipsoid; metacarpophalangeal are condyloid; interphalangeal are hinge synovial joints.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Nerves of Upper Limb core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: All carpometacarpal and intermetacarpal joints are plane types of synovial joints EXCEPT for:
options: The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb
The carpometacarpal joint of the fifth metacarpal
The carpometacarpal joint of the third metacarpal
The intermetacarpal joint of the 4th and 5th metacarpals
questions.explanation: The first carpometacarpal joint (between the trapezium and the base of the first metacarpal of the thumb) is a saddle (sellar) synovial joint, which permits flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and opposition.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Axilla&brachial Plexus core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: Subacromial bursa separates coracoacromial arch from the tendon of:
questions.explanation: The subacromial (subdeltoid) bursa lies between the acromion/coracoacromial ligament superiorly and the tendon of supraspinatus and joint capsule inferiorly, facilitating friction-free abduction of the arm.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Axilla&brachial Plexus core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: The type of the sternoclavicular joint is:
questions.explanation: The sternoclavicular joint is anatomically a saddle (sellar) synovial joint, but functionally moves in all planes like a ball-and-socket joint due to the presence of an intervening fibrocartilaginous articular disc.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Axilla&brachial Plexus core competencies.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.text: Gout is induced by one of the following drugs:
questions.explanation: Thiazide and loop diuretics compete with uric acid for the organic acid secretory transport system in the proximal renal tubules and cause volume depletion, leading to decreased renal clearance of uric acid and drug-induced hyperuricemia/gout.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Gout core competencies.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.text: Indomethacin dose in treatment of acute gouty arthritis is:
questions.explanation: The standard initial dose of indomethacin in acute gouty arthritis is 50 mg orally three times daily (every 8 hours) with meals until joint pain subsides, followed by tapering.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Gout core competencies.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.text: Colchicine chronic adverse effects include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, and vomiting are the hallmark acute gastrointestinal side effects of colchicine toxicity. Bone marrow suppression (leukopenia, neutropenia, aplastic anemia), myopathy, and alopecia are associated with chronic toxic exposure.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Gout core competencies.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.text: Pegloticase is characterized by all of the following except:
options: Should be preceded by antihistamines and corticosteroids
Safe in patients with G6PD deficiency
questions.explanation: Pegloticase (recombinant pegylated uricase) oxidizes uric acid to allantoin and produces hydrogen peroxide as a byproduct. In patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, hydrogen peroxide cannot be neutralized, causing severe acute hemolytic anemia and methemoglobinemia. It is strictly contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Gout core competencies.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.text: Probenecid in low dose may lead to:
questions.explanation: Low-dose probenecid preferentially inhibits the tubular secretion of uric acid without blocking reabsorption, resulting in net uric acid retention and paradoxically worsening hyperuricemia. Full uricosuric therapeutic doses are required to block the URAT1 reabsorption transporter.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Gout core competencies.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.text: Peptic ulceration may be associated with:
questions.explanation: Aspirin, sulfinpyrazone, and glucocorticoids all disrupt gastric mucosal protective barriers by inhibiting mucosal prostaglandin synthesis or impairing epithelial regeneration, predisposing to peptic ulcer disease and GI bleeding.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Gout core competencies.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.text: Colchicine in the treatment of acute gout should be taken:
options: 3 times per day for 3 days after complete recovery
Loading dose followed by hourly or twice-daily dosing until pain relief or GI toxicity
questions.explanation: In acute gout, colchicine is administered as an initial oral loading dose (1.2 mg / 1 mg) followed by 0.6 mg / 0.5 mg one hour later or every 2-3 hours until joint symptoms abate or GI adverse effects (diarrhea/nausea) occur.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Gout core competencies.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.text: Explain why colchicine or low-dose NSAID is added to allopurinol during the first 3 to 6 months of chronic gout treatment.
questions.explanation: Verified pharmacology model answer based on Ain Shams Department Guidelines and Dr. ElShaeir Gout Module.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Gout core competencies.
questions.modelAnswer: Verified pharmacology model answer based on Ain Shams Department Guidelines and Dr. ElShaeir Gout Module.

questions.text: Explain why uricosuric drugs and low-dose Aspirin should NOT be taken during an acute gouty arthritis attack.
questions.explanation: Verified pharmacology model answer based on Ain Shams Department Guidelines and Dr. ElShaeir Gout Module.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Gout core competencies.

questions.text: Outline the long-term pharmacological management of chronic tophaceous gout.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about Staphylococcus aureus is incorrect?
options: Staphylococcal lesions are localized due to coagulase production
Treatment should include a beta-lactamase-resistant penicillin
Endotoxin is an important virulence factor
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive bacterium and therefore completely lacks endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide), which is an exclusive structural component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. Virulence factors of S. aureus include coagulase, protein A, hemolysins, leukocidins, and enterotoxins.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: Skin rash of scarlet fever is mediated by:
questions.explanation: The diffuse erythematous punctate blanching rash of scarlet fever is mediated by lysogenic phage-encoded streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins (erythrogenic toxin A, B, or C) produced by Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS).
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: A 44-year-old male had an open fracture of the right femur and tibia due to a car accident. The patient developed pain, edema, cellulitis, blackening and bad odor at the wound area; Gram-positive bacilli were isolated anaerobically from wound exudates. Which of the following is most probably the causative agent of this infection?
questions.explanation: Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) following contaminated trauma or open fractures is caused by Clostridium perfringens, an anaerobic, spore-forming, Gram-positive bacillus that secretes alpha-toxin (lecithinase), causing gas production (crepitus), foul-smelling exudate, tissue blackening, and rapid necrosis.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) strains are resistant to beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins primarily due to:
options: Degradation of methicillin by a beta-lactamase encoded on a plasmid
Altered penicillin-binding proteins (PBP2a encoded by mecA gene)
questions.explanation: MRSA resistance is mediated by the chromosomal mecA gene, which encodes penicillin-binding protein 2a (PBP2a). PBP2a has remarkably low binding affinity for all beta-lactam antibiotics, permitting cell wall synthesis even in the presence of methicillin, nafcillin, or oxacillin.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: A 4-year-old boy presents with honey-colored crusted skin lesions on his face. Gram stain reveals polymorphs and Gram-positive catalase-negative cocci. If the exudate is cultured on blood agar, which of the following is most likely to be seen?
questions.explanation: Non-bullous impetigo with characteristic honey-colored crusts caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (catalase-negative, Gram-positive cocci in chains) exhibits clear beta-hemolysis (complete lysis of red blood cells) on 5% sheep blood agar and is bacitracin-sensitive.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: Scalded skin syndrome (SSSS / Ritter's disease) is caused by exotoxins (exfoliatins) produced by:
questions.explanation: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is caused by epidermolytic (exfoliative) toxins A and B secreted by Staphylococcus aureus (phage group II), which target and cleave desmoglein-1 in the desmosomes of the stratum granulosum.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following microorganisms causes scarlet fever?
questions.explanation: Scarlet fever is caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus) carrying a temperate bacteriophage that encodes pyrogenic exotoxin / erythrogenic toxin.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of impetigo?
options: Can be caused by Staphylococcus aureus
Can be caused by Streptococcus pyogenes
Can be caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa
questions.explanation: Impetigo is a superficial bacterial skin infection predominantly affecting young children, caused by Staphylococcus aureus and/or Streptococcus pyogenes. It is highly contagious via direct contact but is NOT caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: Bacteria that multiply in blocked skin pores, metabolize sebum, and lead to the development of acne vulgaris are:
options: Acne is not caused by bacterial infection
questions.explanation: Cutibacterium (formerly Propionibacterium) acnes is an anaerobic Gram-positive diphtheroid that colonizes sebaceous follicles, releases lipases that break down triglycerides in sebum into pro-inflammatory free fatty acids, and incites comedone and pustule formation.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: Staphylococcus aureus is most characteristically distinguished from other staphylococci by being:
questions.explanation: Coagulase production (converting fibrinogen to fibrin) is the definitive diagnostic hallmark that distinguishes pathogenic Staphylococcus aureus (coagulase-positive) from coagulase-negative staphylococci such as S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: M protein, a major virulence factor that inhibits phagocytosis by degrading C3b, is produced by:
questions.explanation: M protein is the major cell-wall virulence factor of Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS). It extends as hair-like projections from the cell wall, binds complement regulatory factor H, prevents alternative pathway C3b deposition, and resists opsonophagocytosis.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with skin that is intensely red, raised, shiny, edematous, with a sharply demarcated advancing margin; the most common cause is Group A streptococci. These features are diagnostic of:
questions.explanation: Erysipelas is an acute superficial dermal and lymphatic infection typically caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, characterized by a bright red, swollen, warm, plaque-like lesion with sharply demarcated elevated margins and prominent systemic symptoms (fever, chills).
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: The causative agent of Buruli ulcer (causing extensive necrotizing skin and soft tissue lesions) is:
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium ulcerans produces the lipid-soluble polyketide exotoxin mycolactone, which exerts cytotoxic and immunosuppressive effects, causing severe necrotic subcutaneous destruction known as Buruli ulcer.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: A patient complains to his dentist about a chronic draining sinus in the jaw following dental extraction. A Gram stain of pus shows branching Gram-positive filamentous rods and yellowish 'sulfur granules'. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Cervicofacial actinomycosis, caused by the anaerobic/microaerophilic filamentous Gram-positive bacterium Actinomyces israelii (part of oral flora), produces chronic indurated abscesses with multiple sinus tracts draining purulent material containing characteristic yellow macrocolonies called 'sulfur granules'.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old butcher developed a painless pruritic papule on his forearm that rapidly enlarged, ulcerated, and formed a central depressed black eschar surrounded by non-pitting edema. Gram stain reveals large Gram-positive bacilli with squared ends. The causative organism is:
questions.explanation: Cutaneous anthrax, acquired by direct contact with infected animal carcasses or wool, is caused by Bacillus anthracis (large aerobic Gram-positive spore-forming rod). It classically presents as a painless black necrotic eschar surrounded by extensive gelatinous edema, mediated by lethal toxin and edema toxin.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: A young man suffers major soft tissue trauma and open tibial fractures after a motorcycle accident. On examination, the leg is tense, with thin, foul-smelling dirty brownish discharge, and palpable subcutaneous crepitus. The most likely organism is:
questions.explanation: Palpable crepitus (subcutaneous gas production from carbohydrate fermentation), dirty dishwater discharge, severe muscle pain out of proportion to exam, and rapid tissue necrosis in an open fracture are hallmarks of clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene) caused by Clostridium perfringens.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: A 9-year-old girl presents with fever (39.5°C), sore throat, cervical lymphadenopathy, a diffuse sandpapery erythematous rash that blanches on pressure, and a 'strawberry tongue'. The causative organism is best described as:
questions.explanation: Scarlet fever caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus) is characterized microscopically as Gram-positive cocci in chains, displaying complete beta-hemolysis on blood agar and negative catalase testing.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: A 27-year-old female presents with sudden high fever, vomiting, diarrhea, diffuse sunburn-like macular rash that subsequently desquamates on palms and soles, and hypotension (BP 70/40 mmHg) during her menstrual period while using tampons. Her condition is mediated by:
options: A toxin that hemolyzes red blood cells
A toxin that disrupts intercellular connections of the epidermis
A superantigen toxin that causes massive non-specific activation of T cells and cytokine release
A two-component toxin that forms pores in white blood cells
questions.explanation: Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is mediated by Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin-1 (TSST-1), a superantigen that cross-links the MHC class II receptor on antigen-presenting cells directly to the Vβ domain of T-cell receptors without antigen processing, causing non-specific activation of up to 20% of all T cells and an overwhelming cytokine storm (IL-1, IL-2, TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma).
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy developed a shallow cut on his shin at summer camp. Within 5 days, the area became warm, erythematous, tender, and swollen with poorly demarcated, ill-defined margins that spread rapidly. This condition is most characteristically caused by:
questions.explanation: Cellulitis is an infection of the deep dermis and subcutaneous fat presenting with diffuse, poorly demarcated spreading erythema, warmth, and edema. Group A streptococci (Streptococcus pyogenes) are the most common cause, spreading rapidly through subcutaneous tissue planes by secreting hyaluronidase and streptokinase.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: Urticaria is pathologically mediated by:
options: Type I hypersensitivity (IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation)
Chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease of the skin
questions.explanation: Urticaria (hives) is a Type I IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity reaction characterized by antigen cross-linking of IgE antibodies on mast cells and basophils, triggering release of histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins that produce microvascular hyperpermeability and wheals.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Diseases of Skin core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: A spongiotic intraepidermal pustule (spongiform pustule of Kogoj) is defined as:
options: Small collection of neutrophils within superficial spongiotic epidermis
Small collection of neutrophils within parakeratotic stratum corneum
Small collection of neutrophils below stratum corneum
Small collection of neutrophils within dermal papillae
questions.explanation: A spongiform pustule of Kogoj (characteristic of psoriasis) is an aggregate of neutrophils within the superficial, edematous (spongiotic) spinous layer of the epidermis. Munro microabscesses, by contrast, represent collections of neutrophils in the parakeratotic stratum corneum.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Diseases of Skin core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: Subcorneal pustules are characteristically observed in:
questions.explanation: Subcorneal pustules (blisters situated immediately beneath the stratum corneum) are diagnostic of bullous impetigo, subcorneal pustular dermatosis (Sneddon-Wilkinson disease), and pemphigus foliaceus.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: Papillary microabscesses (aggregates of neutrophils at the dermal papilla tips) are diagnostic of:
questions.explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis is pathognomonic for granular IgA deposition and neutrophilic microabscesses at the tips of dermal papillae, causing dermo-epidermal junction separation and subepidermal microvesicles, associated with celiac disease.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Diseases of Skin core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: Colloid bodies (Civatte bodies / apoptotic keratinocytes) are typically found in:
questions.explanation: Civatte bodies (colloid or cytoid bodies) are anucleate apoptotic basal keratinocytes found in the lower epidermis and upper papillary dermis in lichen planus, resulting from cytotoxic T-cell-mediated basal vacuolar degeneration.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Diseases of Skin core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: Regarding Pemphigus vulgaris, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
options: Antibodies target desmoglein-3 causing loss of intercellular bridges and acantholysis
Basal cells attached to the basement membrane exhibit a 'row of tombstones' appearance
questions.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris produces intraepidermal suprabasal blisters due to IgG antibodies against desmoglein-3 leading to acantholysis (detachment of keratinocytes); the basal layer remains attached to the basement membrane ('tombstone appearance'). Subepidermal blisters are seen in bullous pemphigoid, NOT pemphigus vulgaris.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Diseases of Skin core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: A 20-year-old female presents with a skin eruption composed of well-demarcated erythematous plaques covered by silvery white micaceous scales over both extensor surfaces (elbows and knees):
questions.explanation: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques covered by silvery white scales on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, scalp) that demonstrate Auspitz sign on scraping are classic features of chronic plaque psoriasis vulgaris.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Diseases of Skin core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: Regarding Lichen planus, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
options: Presence of apoptotic Civatte colloid bodies
Loss of the granular cell layer
questions.explanation: Lichen planus is characterized histologically by prominent wedge-shaped hypergranulosis (thickening of the granular layer), NOT loss of the granular layer. Other hallmarks include hyperkeratosis without parakeratosis, sawtooth rete ridges, basal vacuolation, and a dense band-like lymphocytic dermal infiltrate.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Diseases of Skin core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: Seborrheic keratosis is histopathologically characterized by:
options: Horn cysts and pseudo-horn cysts filled with laminated keratin
Peripheral palisading of atypical basaloid cells
questions.explanation: Seborrheic keratosis exhibits benign exophytic proliferation of basaloid keratinocytes with hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, and pathognomonic true horn cysts and pseudo-horn cysts (invaginations of stratum corneum filled with concentric keratin).
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Diseases of Skin core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: Actinic (solar) keratosis is histologically characterized by:
options: Atypical, dysplastic keratinocytes confined to the lower epidermis (basal and lower spinous layers)
Loss of the granular layer and uniform full-thickness atypia
Involvement of deep skin adnexal epithelium
questions.explanation: Actinic keratosis (a premalignant precursor to squamous cell carcinoma induced by UV radiation) shows cellular atypia, pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and loss of polarity confined to the lower basal and spinous layers of the epidermis, often accompanied by overlying alternating parakeratosis/orthokeratosis and solar elastosis in the dermis.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Diseases of Skin core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: Eosinophilic microabscesses within subepidermal blisters are characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by subepidermal blisters containing eosinophils, linear IgG and C3 deposition along the dermo-epidermal junction targeting hemidesmosomal BP180/BP230 antigens, and eosinophilic microabscesses in the papillary dermis.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Diseases of Skin core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: Neutrophilic microabscesses localized specifically at the tips of dermal papillae are seen in:
questions.explanation: Collections of neutrophils at the apex (tips) of dermal papillae accompanied by granular IgA deposits on direct immunofluorescence are pathognomonic for dermatitis herpetiformis.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Diseases of Skin core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: Lichen planus is characterized histologically by which of the following epidermal alterations?
questions.explanation: Hypergranulosis (thickening of the stratum granulosum) is a classic histological feature of lichen planus, producing the clinically visible fine white lines known as Wickham's striae on the surfaces of violaceous polygonal pruritic papules.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Diseases of Skin core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: A 75-year-old male presents with a slow-growing, sharply demarcated, pigmented exophytic plaque with a greasy, verrucous surface on his shoulder that appears 'stuck on'. Excision and histopathology demonstrate sheets of uniform small basaloid cells surrounding circular keratin-filled cysts. The diagnosis is:
options: Bowen disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ)
questions.explanation: A pigmented 'stuck-on' plaque with a greasy/keratotic surface containing sheets of benign basaloid cells and keratin-filled horn cysts without cytological atypia is diagnostic of seborrheic keratosis.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Diseases of Skin core competencies.

questions.text: The following is incorrect regarding Misoprostol
options: Used to avoid development of analgesic ulcer
Increases rhythmic contraction of the uterus
Is a PG E analogue Cross MATCH each prostaglandin analogs to its adverse effect
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C: Decreases GIT motility. Verified from Part 1 Model Answer Key (Page 57).
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Nsaids core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: The cell of origin of Ewing's sarcoma is:
questions.explanation: Ewing sarcoma is a highly malignant primitive neuroectodermal tumor (PNET) arising from postganglionic parasympathetic neuroectodermal primordial cells in the bone marrow cavity, characterized by t(11;22)(q24;q12) translocation generating the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion oncogene and strong CD99 membrane positivity.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Tumors core competencies.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.text: Tophi in chronic gout result from deposition of:
questions.explanation: Gouty tophi are pathognomonic nodular aggregates of needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals surrounded by an intense foreign body giant cell granulomatous inflammatory reaction in articular cartilage, synovial membranes, tendons, and subcutaneous periarticular tissues.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Gout core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is inherited as:
options: X-linked recessive deficit in dystrophin gene
questions.explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by out-of-frame deletion or nonsense mutations in the DMD gene on chromosome Xp21, resulting in complete absence of the sarcolemmal structural protein dystrophin.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Muscle Disorders core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: The commonest primary malignant tumor arising in bone overall is:
questions.explanation: Multiple myeloma (plasma cell myeloma) is the most common primary malignant neoplasm involving bone in adults over 50 years of age. If hematological malignancies are excluded, osteosarcoma is the most common non-hematopoietic primary malignant bone sarcoma.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Tumors core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: A biopsy from a vertebral lesion reveals a cellular malignant proliferation with homogenous pink stroma that exhibits apple-green birefringence under polarized light when stained positively by Congo red. The cell of origin of this tumor is:
questions.explanation: A bone biopsy demonstrating neoplastic plasma cells with Congo red-positive amyloid stroma represents AL (amyloid light chain) amyloidosis complicating multiple myeloma (plasma cell myeloma).
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Tumors core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: The most diagnostic microscopic hallmark of osteosarcoma is:
options: Spindle cell proliferation with atypical mitoses
Direct production of unmineralized osteoid matrix by malignant mesenchymal cells
questions.explanation: The sine qua non histological diagnostic criterion for osteosarcoma is the direct production of osteoid (unmineralized immature woven bone) or bone matrix by malignant pleomorphic osteoblastic stromal cells.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Tumors core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: Which of the following bone tumor cells characteristically stains strongly positive with Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) due to abundant cytoplasmic glycogen:
questions.explanation: Ewing sarcoma cells are uniform, small round blue cells with clear to pale cytoplasm that is rich in glycogen, which stains strongly positive with Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) and is diastase-sensitive.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Diseases of Skin core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: Paget disease of bone (osteitis deformans) may be complicated systemically by:
questions.explanation: In the polyostotic hypervascular phase of Paget disease, extensive arteriovenous shunting within newly formed vascular pagetic bone creates marked decreases in peripheral vascular resistance, leading to high-output congestive heart failure.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Non-tumor Diseases of Bone core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: The most common malignant neoplasm complicating preexisting Paget disease of bone in elderly patients is:
questions.explanation: Secondary osteosarcoma occurs in approximately 1% of patients with Paget disease of bone, typically in patients over 65 years of age, presenting as new severe bone pain, rapidly enlarging mass, and destructive lytic cortical lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Non-tumor Diseases of Bone core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: Brown tumor of bone is a localized reactive bone lesion caused by:
options: Primary or secondary hyperparathyroidism (Osteitis fibrosa cystica)
questions.explanation: Brown tumors of bone (osteitis fibrosa cystica / Recklinghausen disease of bone) result from excess parathyroid hormone (hyperparathyroidism) stimulating osteoclastic bone resorption with microfractures, secondary hemorrhage, and hemosiderin pigment accumulation that imparts a gross brown color.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Diseases of Skin core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: A characteristic 'mosaic pattern' of bone lamellae separated by prominent irregular cement lines resembling a jigsaw puzzle is pathognomonic for:
questions.explanation: The histological hallmark of Paget disease of bone is the mosaic or jigsaw-puzzle pattern of trabecular bone, produced by chaotic waves of osteoclastic resorption coupled with haphazard osteoblastic woven bone deposition, demarcated by irregular scalloped basophilic cement reversal lines.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Non-tumor Diseases of Bone core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: All of the following chronic inflammatory conditions may be complicated by secondary (AA) amyloidosis EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Secondary (reactive system) AA amyloidosis occurs as a complication of persistent chronic suppurative or granulomatous inflammation (tuberculosis/Pott's disease, chronic osteomyelitis, rheumatoid arthritis, bronchiectasis). Osteomalacia is a metabolic vitamin D deficiency state without chronic inflammation and cannot cause AA amyloidosis.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bone&joint Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: Septic arthritis may directly complicate acute hematogenous osteomyelitis through intra-articular extension in joints where the metaphysis is located within the joint capsule, most notably the:
questions.explanation: In the hip joint (and shoulder), the metaphysis of the proximal femur lies entirely intracapsular within the joint capsule. Consequently, a subperiosteal abscess arising from acute metaphyseal osteomyelitis can easily rupture directly into the joint cavity, causing secondary septic arthritis.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bone&joint Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: In osteomyelitis, the pathological term 'involucrum' refers to:
options: Dead cortical bone separated from its blood supply
A sleeve of newly formed reactive subperiosteal living bone encasing necrotic bone
A discharging sinus tract draining pus to the skin surface
A bone cavity remaining after surgical sequestrectomy
questions.explanation: Involucrum is a sheath or sleeve of living, irregular, reactive subperiosteal woven bone formed by the elevated periosteum around necrotic, infected devitalized cortical bone (the sequestrum).
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bone&joint Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: The term 'Brodie abscess' in bone pathology refers to:
options: A cold caseous abscess in the retropharyngeal space secondary to cervical spine TB
A purulent joint effusion in acute gonococcal arthritis
A subcutaneous abscess complicating soft tissue cellulitis
A chronic localized intraosseous cortical or metaphyseal abscess surrounded by dense sclerotic bone
questions.explanation: A Brodie abscess is a chronic, localized form of subacute or chronic pyogenic osteomyelitis, typically located in the metaphysis of long bones (especially the proximal tibia), characterized by a small focus of purulent liquefactive necrosis enclosed by a dense wall of reactive sclerotic bone and granulation tissue.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bone&joint Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.text: A 50-year-old male presents with deep aching pain in his right knee and neck that is worse at the end of the day after physical activity and relieved by rest. Examination reveals joint crepitus without warmth, erythema, or systemic fever. ESR and rheumatoid factor are normal. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Osteoarthritis is a non-inflammatory degenerative 'wear-and-tear' arthropathy characterized by articular cartilage loss, subchondral bone sclerosis (eburnation), subchondral cysts, osteophyte formation, joint crepitus, and mechanical pain that worsens with joint use and improves with rest.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Gout core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents with persistent pain and swelling of the distal thigh and knee. Plain radiographs demonstrate an eccentric, well-circumscribed lytic lesion in the epiphysis extending into the metaphysis with a 'soap-bubble' appearance. Biopsy reveals multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells distributed uniformly among mononuclear stromal cells. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Giant cell tumor of bone (osteoclastoma) is a benign but locally aggressive epiphyseal neoplasm classically occurring in skeletal maturity (ages 20-40) around the knee (distal femur or proximal tibia), showing eccentric lytic 'soap-bubble' destruction radiographically and sheets of multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells microscopically.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Tumors core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: A 70-year-old male presents with knee pain. Radiographs reveal an ill-defined destructive osteolytic mass in the distal femur with punctate, ring-and-arc, 'popcorn-like' calcifications and cortical endosteal scalloping. Biopsy reveals atypical, hyperchromatic chondrocytes with binucleation and abundant hyaline matrix. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Chondrosarcoma is a malignant cartilage-producing bone neoplasm occurring predominantly in older adults (>50 years), characterized radiologically by endosteal scalloping and 'popcorn' rings-and-arcs chondroid matrix mineralization, and histologically by malignant pleomorphic chondrocytes in a cartilaginous matrix without direct osteoid formation.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Tumors core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: A 63-year-old male with small cell lung carcinoma develops progressive proximal muscle weakness that paradoxically improves temporarily with repeated muscle contraction. Deep tendon reflexes are depressed. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is a paraneoplastic autoimmune channelopathy strongly associated with small cell lung cancer, mediated by autoantibodies against P/Q-type presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, leading to reduced acetylcholine exocytosis and proximal weakness that improves with exertion.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Muscle Disorders core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: A 53-year-old male has noted a slowly enlarging, firm subcutaneous nodule over his olecranon bursa for the past 2 years. Biopsy reveals needle-shaped crystalline deposits surrounded by a granulomatous inflammatory reaction with foreign body giant cells. Which laboratory abnormality is most consistently associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: Gouty tophi with negative birefringent needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals surrounded by histiocytic giant cell granulomas develop as a consequence of prolonged, unmanaged hyperuricemia (serum urate >6.8 mg/dL).
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Joint Diseases core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: A 36-year-old female presents with bilateral, symmetric pain and swelling of the PIP and MCP joints with prolonged morning stiffness (>1 hour) and ulnar deviation. Synovial biopsy reveals marked papillary synovial hyperplasia, intense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with lymphoid follicles, and an invasive inflammatory granulation tissue mass that erodes underlying articular cartilage and subchondral bone. This destructive tissue is known as:
questions.explanation: In rheumatoid arthritis, chronic synovial inflammation stimulates the formation of a pannus—an invasive, proliferative fibrovascular inflammatory membrane composed of synovial cells, CD4+ T cells, plasma cells, and macrophages producing TNF-alpha, IL-1, and collagenases that degrade cartilage and underlying bone.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Joint Diseases core competencies.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: A 20-year-old male presents with localized pain and swelling above his right knee for 2 months. Plain radiographs show a destructive osteolytic and osteoblastic lesion at the lower end of the right femur with irregular bony spicules perpendicular to the cortex ('sunburst' appearance) and a triangular lifting of the periosteum ('Codman triangle'). Provide the clinical analysis, age distribution, microscopic pathology, and complications.
questions.explanation: Official pathology clinical case analysis verified from Dr. Tarek El Shamy Ain Shams University Pathology Department.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Tumors core competencies.
questions.modelAnswer: Official pathology clinical case analysis verified from Dr. Tarek El Shamy Ain Shams University Pathology Department.

questions.subject: pathology
questions.text: A 60-year-old male presents with severe, progressive mid-thoracic back pain and fatigue. Plain radiographs reveal well-demarcated 'punched-out' osteolytic lesions in the T4 and T5 vertebral bodies without sclerotic margins. Laboratory investigations demonstrate hypercalcemia, normocytic anemia, renal impairment, and monoclonal light chains (Bence Jones proteins) on serum and urine protein electrophoresis. Provide the complete medical assessment.
questions.explanation: Official pathology clinical case analysis verified from Dr. Tarek El Shamy Ain Shams University Pathology Department.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Tumors core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: Bacterial pathogens commonly associated with infected dog and cat bites include:
questions.explanation: Pasteurella multocida is a small Gram-negative coccobacillus that is part of the normal oral flora of domestic cats (up to 90%) and dogs (up to 50%), causing rapidly progressive, severe cellulitis, tenosynovitis, and osteomyelitis within 24 hours of animal bite injuries.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: Leprosy (Hansen disease) is definitive diagnosed microscopically by demonstrating acid-fast bacilli in:
options: A sputum smear stained with Gram stain
A slit-skin smear or dermal biopsy stained with modified Ziehl-Neelsen (Fite-Faraco) stain
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium leprae is an obligate intracellular acid-fast bacillus that cannot be cultured in vitro on artificial media (including Lowenstein-Jensen). Definitive diagnosis relies on demonstrating acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smears from earlobes/lesions or skin/nerve biopsies using modified Ziehl-Neelsen (Fite-Faraco) staining.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: microbiology
questions.text: The clinical and pathological spectrum of leprosy (Hansen disease) is primarily determined by:
options: The host cell-mediated immune (CMI) response to Mycobacterium leprae
The direct necrotizing exotoxins produced by M. leprae
questions.explanation: The manifestations of Hansen disease range along a clinical spectrum dictated entirely by the host's cell-mediated immunity (CMI): strong Th1 CMI produces Tuberculoid leprosy (few hypopigmented anesthetic lesions, granulomas, few bacilli); while deficient Th1 / Th2-skewed immunity leads to Lepromatous leprosy (diffuse infiltrative leonine facies, loss of sensation, massive bacillary burden in globi).
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Bacterial Skin Infections core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: One of the following muscles is attached to the iliotibial tract:
questions.explanation: The iliotibial tract receives the insertion of the tensor fasciae latae anteriorly and the upper three-quarters (superficial fibers) of the gluteus maximus posteriorly, transmitting tension across the lateral aspect of the thigh and knee to stabilize the erect posture.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Front of Thigh core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are functions of the iliotibial tract EXCEPT:
options: Helps maintain the knee extended when standing upright
Helps in rising from a sitting position through gluteus maximus
Allows passive lateral rotation of the knee when flexed
Stabilizes the pelvis on the femoral head during unilateral stance
questions.explanation: The iliotibial tract acts as a major lateral stabilizer of the hip and knee joints during standing and walking, bracing the knee in extension. It does not allow passive lateral rotation of the knee when flexed.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Knee core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: The articularis genu muscle is anatomically derived from and attached to:
options: Deep fibers of vastus intermedius inserting into the synovial suprapatellar bursa
questions.explanation: Articularis genu consists of a few muscular slips derived from the deep surface of the vastus intermedius that insert into the upper part of the suprapatellar synovial bursa, pulling the synovial membrane superiorly during knee extension to prevent its entrapment between the femur and patella.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Front of Thigh core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: The medial boundary of the femoral triangle is formed by the:
questions.explanation: The boundaries of the femoral triangle are: Superiorly by the inguinal ligament; Laterally by the medial border of sartorius; and Medially by the medial border of adductor longus (some anatomists describe the medial boundary as the adductor longus muscle itself).
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Front of Thigh core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: In an injury or complete lesion of the femoral nerve in the femoral triangle, all of the following neurological signs may be found EXCEPT:
options: Loss of the patellar tendon reflex (knee jerk)
Inability to extend the knee against gravity
Loss of cutaneous sensation over the anteromedial thigh and medial side of the leg
Loss of cutaneous sensation over the lateral side of the big toe
questions.explanation: The femoral nerve supplies the quadriceps femoris (loss of knee extension and knee jerk) and gives off the anterior cutaneous nerves of thigh and the saphenous nerve (supplying skin on medial thigh, medial leg, and medial border of the foot up to the medial side of the ball of the big toe). The lateral side of the big toe and first webspace is supplied by the deep peroneal (fibular) nerve, NOT the femoral nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Knee core competencies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.text: A 75-year-old female slips on the floor and falls, sustaining a subcapital fracture of the femoral neck. Total hip replacement is recommended because subcapital fractures carry an extremely high risk of:
options: Avascular osteonecrosis of the femoral head due to disruption of retinacular branches of medial circumflex femoral artery
Severe damage to the sciatic nerve
questions.explanation: The primary arterial blood supply to the femoral head is provided by ascending cervical (retinacular) branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery running beneath the capsule. Subcapital and transcervical fractures of the femoral neck rupture these intracapsular retinacular vessels, cutting off blood supply and leading to avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head in up to 30-50% of cases.
questions.keyConcept: Ain Shams Locomotor Module: Gluteal Region core competencies.
